newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr on solid base after steady week.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr on solid base after steady week.

text.p: The Australian dollar wound down a week of steady consolidation in suitably composed style Friday and kept a firm grip on the 81 cent level.
The currency was working out a heavily overbought position after last week's wildly impulsive 2-1/2 cent rally and further restrained by options-related offers in the US$0.8130/50 area.
Dealers, however, were impressed by the lack of a substantial correction and looked for a resumption of the uptrend toward US$0.8240 and, eventually, US$0.8450.
Current account data showed a 6.0 percent widening in the deficit, but the market was largely inured to such shortfalls.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local currency was making itself at home at US$0.8106/11 from an early US$0.8100/05 and US$0.8095/00 late here Thursday.
Support and resistance were well defined at US$0.8075 and US$0.8130 and dealers doubted either would be troubled offshore with the U.S. market thinned by Thanksgiving.
There was still a risk of a pullback to US$0.8030/50 but it would take a break of US$0.7950 to dull the bullish mood.
The outlook was equally upbeat on the crosses where the dollar extended its rally to a fresh four year high of 92.48 yen this morning before easing back to close at 92.05/15.
That was still up on Thursday's late 91.56/66 yen and a whole 2.2 percent higher than last Friday's finish.
In trade weighted terms the currency hit 60.0 on its index for the first time since October 1991, before edging back to 59.9 but again was up on Thursday's 59.8 and last week's 59.4.

Analysts doubted it would stop there as the sluggishness of the Japanese economy -- as illustrated by the cautious Q3 Tankan survey released on Wednesday -- meant interest rates would stay at record lows for some months yet.
Japanese data today reinforced the sober outlook with unemployment rising to 3.4 percent in October from 3.3 percent.
National consumer prices rose 0.2 percent, which was above forecasts of a 0.1 percent fall, but was balanced by a surprise 0.3 percent drop in Tokyo's CPI.

With Japanese rates set to remain low, analysts said there was every reason to expect further Japanese demand for higher yielding yen/A$ dual currency samurai bonds which in turn would underpin the dollar's gains.

Today's balance of payments data suggested the current account deficit may return to haunt markets next year, although analysts had their suspicions about a 9.0 percent deterioration in the net income deficit to A$1.91 billion in October.

This was the major factor in the widening of the current account deficit to A$1.788 billion from A$1.690 billion in September. This was above expectations of A$1.6 billion and the fourth month in a row when the deficit had risen.
However, the income figuires were based on extrapolations from the past and were likely to be revised -- probably downwards -- when foreign investment data were known next month.

The merchandise trade position was essentially in balance with both exports and imports rising around 1.0 percent and analysts looked for exports to be boosted by a near record wheat crop which will all be shifted in the next couple of months.
Analysts said the data had no implications for monetary policy and were awaiting next week's helping of real side figures to refine their thinking on wether the Reserve Bank will cut rates again.
The releases include retail trade and building approvals for October, private sector inventories for Q3 and the September quarter GDP report.
The Reserve Bank also held its December board meeting Tuesday, but few saw much chance of them sanctioning a cut in rates so soon after the last easing on November 6.
